summary: DLMF 1.17 Integral and Series Representations of the Dirac Delta: In applications in physics, engineering, and applied mathematics, (see Friedman ( 1990 ) ), the Dirac delta…
body: NIST DLMF section 1.17 (Integral and Series Representations of the Dirac Delta) says: "In applications in physics, engineering, and applied mathematics, (see Friedman ( 1990 ) ), the Dirac delta distribution (§ 1.16(iii) ) is historically and customarily replaced by the Dirac delta (or Dirac delta function ) \delta\left(x\right) . This is a symbolic function with the properties: subject to certain conditions on the function \phi(x) . From the mathematical standpoint the left-hand side of ( 1.17.2 ) can be interpreted as a generalized integral in the sense that for a suitably chosen sequence of functions \delta_{n}\left(x\right) , n=1,2,\dots . Such a sequence is called a delta sequence and we write, symbolically, An example of a delta sequence is provided by for all functions \phi(x) that are continuous when x\in(-\infty,\infty) , and for each a , \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}{\mathrm{e}}^{-n(x-a)^{2}}\phi(x)\,\mathrm{d}x converges absolutely for all sufficiently large values of n . The last condition is satisfied, for example, when \phi(x)=O\left({\mathrm{e}}^{\alpha x^{2}}\right) as x\to\pm\infty , where \alpha is a real constant." Equation 1.17.1 on the page has alt text "\delta\left(x\right)=0,". Equation 1.17.2 on the page has alt text "\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta\left(x-a\right)\phi(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\phi(a),". This card records that section's wording and equation alt text. It does not retypeset a formula the alt text did not carry.
